svg.font-family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Figure 1. Two doors into the same account
svg.desc: A comparison of the sign in path and the recovery path. The sign in path is the one you spent three lessons hardening, with a password manager, a hardware key and the weaker methods removed. The recovery path was designed by somebody else, to a different standard, for a person who has genuinely lost everything, and you did not choose it. Both open the same account, so the account's strength is the weaker of the two. A band below reframes the usual trade: the choice is not between security and recoverability, but between fast recovery and safe recovery, and safe recovery is slow, noisy and arranged in advance.
svg.text: Figure 1: Two Doors Into the Same Account
Three lessons went into the door on the left. The door on the right came with the building, and it opens onto the same room.
the sign in path, from Lessons 4.1 to 4.3

g.text: A unique password from a vault you chose. A hardware
key, or a passkey. The weaker methods removed.
You did, deliberately, over three lessons, against a
You, on an ordinary day, signing in as normal.

svg.text: THE DOOR THAT CAME WITH IT
the recovery path, which you have probably never read

g.text: Frequently a link to an email address, a code by text
message, a date of birth, or a person on a telephone.
A product team balancing support costs against fraud,
to a standard you were not consulted on.
A distressed person who has genuinely lost everything.

svg.text: Both doors open the same account, so the account is exactly as strong as the weaker of the two.
Everything in Lessons 4.1 to 4.3 raised the left one. This lesson is about the fact that nobody checks the right one.
The usual framing of this problem is wrong, and the correct one tells you what to do
You will read that recovery is a trade between security and recoverability: lock it down and risk losing it forever, or keep it easy and let attackers in. That framing
makes the problem look unsolvable. It is not the actual trade.
The trade is between fast recovery and safe recovery. A recovery path can be completely reliable and still be hostile to an attacker, if it is:

g.text: Slow. A delay of hours costs you an afternoon once in a decade. It costs an attacker the entire operation, because you are notified while it runs.
Noisy. Every step announces itself to you on a channel the attacker does not control. Recovery starting is the alert that matters most.
Arranged in advance. It uses something you set up while calm, not something you can talk a stranger into accepting while distressed.

svg.text: This is not theoretical. One large platform now imposes an hour of delay and a second biometric check before an account password or a recovery method
can be changed away from familiar locations, precisely so a thief with your device and your passcode cannot lock you out before you react.
Slow, noisy and pre-arranged. That is the design goal for every recovery path you control.
